summary: Mission Beyond is a browser-based Space Mission Design Game built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Players design a spacecraft within a real budget (mass, power, data, radiation), launch it, then fly it through a day-by-day simulation of solar storms, computer faults and ground-network outages. A walkable “Command Deck” hub — move with arrow keys, WASD, or a touch D-pad — connects four build consoles and the launch pad, so the whole experience plays like a game rather than a form. Every technical check carries a plain-language explanation underneath it, and a story-style mission briefing introduces each mission’s purpose and audience before building starts, making real NASA fact-sheet physics approachable for secondary-school-age players and up. It’s a static site with no backend, no account and no install.
details:
Github: https://github.com/mdsba12/MissionBeyond

  1. How Mission Beyond Works
    The game runs entirely in the browser — vanilla JavaScript, HTML and CSS, no build step, no dependencies. It has been tested in modern desktop and mobile browsers at both narrow (phone) and wide (desktop) viewport sizes with no layout overflow.

Campaign structure: four missions unlock one at a time (Earth Watch, Lunar Ice, Red Weather, Ocean Moon), each tied to a real science question. Each is scored out of 100 with up to three stars based on how cleanly it was flown.

  1. The Command Deck (walkable hub)
    A pixel-art commander walks between five consoles — Launch, Spacecraft, Ground, Operations, and the launch pad — steered by arrow keys, WASD, or an on-screen D-pad on touch devices. Walking up to a console (or tapping it) opens it; there’s nothing to get stuck on.
  2. The Build Bay
    Every part added to the design costs mass, power, money or data, and a live set of checks (budget, launch-mass margin, power balance, data link, radiation shielding) updates immediately. Each check is shown with both its technical readout and a second, child-friendly sentence explaining why it matters.
  3. The Flight Simulation
    A real day-by-day simulation advances the mission: power generation versus load, onboard data buffer and downlink contact windows, pointing accuracy, and randomized solar-storm events that are forecast two days ahead. Incidents arrive as readable pop-ups with real consequences for the final score. A compact repair-panel widget gives an at-a-glance GOOD / CAUTION / BAD system status, driven entirely by the live simulation state.
  4. Accessibility & Audience
    A slide-deck-style tutorial (skippable, replayable) and per-mission briefings explain what the mission is, why it matters, and a suggested age range before the player is asked to do anything. Plain-language captions sit alongside every technical readout rather than replacing it, so the game works for both a complete beginner and someone who wants the real numbers.
  5. Data Integrity
    Every numeric constant used in the simulation (orbital parameters, instrument power draws, data rates, radiation thresholds) is tagged in the source code as either sourced from a NASA fact sheet or explicitly marked as a game-balance assumption. An automated check runs before every release to confirm no untagged numbers have crept in.
  6. Tech Stack
    Vanilla JavaScript (ES modules), hand-drawn pixel-art sprites and canvas rendering, CSS for the pixel-frame UI system, Node’s built-in test runner (38 passing tests covering the physics, engine and simulation logic). No frameworks, no build tooling, no backend — deployable as a static site (e.g. GitHub Pages).
